subject: Banking
title: Why Companies Need Investment Banks
description: Learn Why Companies Need Investment Banks in one minute.

hook.text: A company can raise money alone, but without a bank it must find buyers, set price, and absorb mistrust.

buildup.text: Bankers bring distribution, industry knowledge, and underwriting, which is why companies pay huge fees.

discovery.text: They also provide credibility. An IPO backed by Goldman Sachs signals quality.

twist.text: Spotify bypassed banks with a direct listing in 2018. It proved some companies can skip the intermediary entirely.

climax.text: Investment banks sell access, expertise, and trust. When companies have all three already, the bank becomes optional.

punchline.text: Banks sell trust and access. Some companies no longer need it.

quiz.question: How did Spotify challenge the traditional investment bank model?
options: It bypassed banks with a direct listing

details.summary: Companies need investment banks because raising billions in capital, executing multi-billion-dollar mergers, and navigating complex securities regulations require specialized expertise, relationships, and distribution networks that companies lack internally.
details.whyItMatters: Investment banks are financial intermediaries that connect companies needing capital with investors who have it. Without them, the massive scale of modern capital markets and corporate deal-making would not function efficiently.
takeaways: Banks provide valuation, distribution, and regulatory expertise
Their investor relationships enable access to institutional capital
Companies rarely have internal capability for billion-dollar transactions

faq.question: Could companies raise capital without investment banks?
faq.answer: For small amounts, yes through direct listings or crowdfunding. But raising billions requires the distribution network, regulatory expertise, and institutional investor relationships that only major investment banks possess.

faq.question: Are investment banking fees justified?
faq.answer: For large transactions, the fees are typically less than 2 percent of deal value. Given the complexity, risk, and capital required, most companies consider these fees reasonable relative to the amount of money raised or the deal size involved.
